title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
description: Find a value in a sorted list that was rotated at an unknown point, in O(log n).
statement:
A list of **distinct** integers sorted in ascending order was rotated at an unknown point: some elements from the front were moved to the back, keeping their order. For example `[0, 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7]` can become `[4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2]`.

Given the rotated list `nums` and a `target`, return the index of `target`, or `-1` if it is not in the list.

- The list may be empty (return `-1`), and it may not be rotated at all.
- Aim for **O(log n)**. The last tests pass a sequence of a billion numbers that supports only `len(nums)` and `nums[i]` and count how many elements you look at, so scanning or copying it will not work.

**Examples**

```python
search_rotated([4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2], 0)   # 4
search_rotated([4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2], 3)   # -1
search_rotated([1], 1)                     # 0
```
hints: A plain binary search needs a sorted list, and this one is sorted only in pieces. Is any part of the list still sorted when you look at the middle?

At every step at least one half (`lo..mid` or `mid..hi`) is sorted. Compare `nums[lo]` with `nums[mid]` to tell which, check whether the target falls inside that half's range, and keep the half that can contain it.

With two elements `lo` and `mid` are the same position, so compare `nums[lo] <= nums[mid]` with `<=`. When you test the sorted half's range, `mid` has already been compared with the target, so leave it out of the range.
explanation:
**The idea.** After a rotation the list as a whole is no longer sorted, but at every step **one of the two halves is**. Compare `nums[lo]` with `nums[mid]` to find which: if `nums[lo] <= nums[mid]` the left half is sorted, otherwise the right half is. Then check whether the target lies inside that sorted half's range. If it does, keep that half; if not, it can only be in the other one. Either way half of the list is gone, so the search is O(log n).

**The details people get wrong.** Use `<=` when comparing `nums[lo]` with `nums[mid]`: on a two-element range `lo` and `mid` are the same position, and a single element counts as sorted. Be exact at the edges of the range check too: `mid` was already compared with the target, so exclude it (`nums[lo] <= target < nums[mid]` and `nums[mid] < target <= nums[hi]`).

**Another way.** Find the rotation point first (see Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array), then run an ordinary binary search on the part of the list that can hold the target.

**Complexity.** O(log n) time, O(1) space.

**Follow-up.** What if the list can contain duplicates? When `nums[lo] == nums[mid] == nums[hi]` you cannot tell which half is sorted, and the worst case falls back to O(n).
